#5081. Pressure Mounts on Nvidia's Jensen Huang Amid Reports of Second Affair

Pressure Mounts on Nvidia's Jensen Huang Amid Reports of Second Affair

Nvidia's board is preparing to remove CEO Jensen Huang after reports that he had two extramarital affairs, one with a woman U.S. intelligence believes is a Chinese spy and another with a company executive, The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday.

The board was planning to meet as soon as Wednesday to determine Huang's future, according to people familiar with the matter cited by the Journal. It was not immediately clear who would succeed him, the paper said.

The New York Times reported on Wednesday that Huang had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care, who reports to him, citing five people who worked at the company. The Journal also reported the relationship, citing a person familiar with the matter.

Nvidia's code of conduct tells employees to avoid situations that create conflicts, including personal relationships, according to the Times. When the newspaper reached him by phone, Huang said, "I don't think you should be talking to me directly," before hanging up. Nvidia declined to comment, and Powell did not respond to requests for comment from either paper.

It is the second affair involving Huang to come to light. The New York Times reported in October that U.S. officials had concluded Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based Nvidia customer Megaspeed, was a Chinese intelligence asset who had developed a close relationship with Jensen Huang. The Financial Times reported last week that a U.S. government memo said the two had been romantically involved. China has denied the allegations.

On Sunday, Huang acknowledged in a letter to staff that he had been unfaithful to his wife, without naming the person involved. He had told Nvidia's board that he had been intimate with Alice Huang, the Times reported, prompting the board to open an independent investigation, led by law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz.

The Justice Department is now leading multiple investigations involving Alice Huang, the Journal reported. Huang also faces a proposed shareholder class action and the threat of a congressional subpoena.

Nvidia shares were down 5.9% at $163.43 in premarket trading early on Thursday, according to Yahoo! Finance data, after closing up 2.9% at $173.73 on Wednesday, before the reports emerged. The stock had already lost about $430 billion in market value on Monday and Tuesday.

Traders expect further losses. On Decrypt Predict, users put an 89% chance on Nvidia trading at or below $160 during regular market hours at some point in November, according to the market. By contrast, they gave just a 6% chance that the stock would climb back to $216 this month.

Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and is its largest shareholder, owning about 3.6% of the company. He has said he does not believe in succession planning, according to the Journal, and the company's latest proxy statement warns that it is "highly dependent" on its longstanding executive team, raising questions over who could replace him.

Potential successors are reportedly under discussion already. One person inside the company told the Financial Times that the simplest option would be to appoint chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim CEO, while two sources pointed to Ian Buck, who runs Nvidia's data center business. Analysts cited Arm CEO Rene Haas, a former Nvidia executive, as a possible outside candidate. "We always knew key man risk was an issue for Nvidia," Bernstein analyst Stacy Rasgon told the paper.

At least one high-profile figure has offered Huang a way forward. Responding to a tweet urging him to hire Huang, Tesla CEO Elon Musk wrote: "That would be an honor."

#5078. A forced Bitcoin Lightning exit can be cheap and still leave you waiting days

A study of public channels found a median force-close cost of 925 satoshis across both sides. The party who closed the channel waited a median 2.5 days before they could sweep their balance.

When a Bitcoin Lightning channel closes without both parties agreeing, the fees can be small but the wait can stretch for days. In a 2026 sample of public channels, forced closures cost a median 925 satoshis per channel across both parties, while the party that initiated the closure waited a median 2.5 days before it could reclaim its own balance, according to Saurabh Kumar's November 12 preprint.

Kumar, of Bitcoin Data Labs, reports 973,581 channel closes from January 2018 through October 31, 2026, including 523,815 force closes. The detailed 2026 cost cohort covers 14,435 public force closes through October 4, leaving four weeks to follow their outputs.

For comparison, the paper reports a 2026 cooperative-close median of 197 satoshis. The ratio between the force-close and cooperative-close medians was 4.7 to one. Its force-close total includes the commitment transaction, required balance sweeps, pending-payment resolution, observed same-block owner fee bumps and later owner anchor cleanup, with batched spending fees divided among inputs.

A unilateral close uses a previously signed commitment transaction to settle a channel on Bitcoin. Under Lightning's BOLT 3 specification, the output returning the broadcaster's own balance carries a delay called to_self_delay. That gives the peer time to penalize a broadcaster that submits a revoked channel state.

The 2.5-day figure measures the wait before that balance becomes eligible to be swept. It does not promise receipt in a wallet at that moment, and it does not describe the speed of ordinary Lightning payments. Across the whole study period, the reported median wait was 1.7 days.

In the preprint's 2026 public force-close cohort, a small miner-fee bill came with a separate delay for the broadcaster's own balance.

A fee-paying child funds the commitment package. The broadcaster's balance delay remains.

HTLC resolution transactions obtain their mining fees through additional inputs.

Paying the settlement fee does not remove the broadcaster's contractual wait.

Fees aggregate both parties per channel. Delay ends at sweep eligibility, not wallet receipt. Excludes private cooperative closes and unclassified simple-taproot spending details. Zero-fee mechanism panel is protocol context, not cohort-specific evidence.

Reported 2026 cohort medians, not a simulation: 14,435 public force closes through October 4. Timeline geometry is schematic and not a time scale. Fee-route diagrams separately explain the BOLT 3 zero-fee design, not outcomes measured for that design.

Fees aggregate both parties per channel. Delay ends at sweep eligibility, not wallet receipt. Excludes private cooperative closes and unclassified simple-taproot spending details. Zero-fee mechanism panel is protocol context, not cohort-specific evidence.

This distinction matters for operators that need accessible funds while a channel is settling. A cheap exit can still leave capital unavailable for days; its fee alone does not reveal how much immediately usable liquidity remains.

Kumar compares those costs using a break-even annual return: the rate at which the broadcaster's locked-balance waiting cost would equal force-close fees. It was 1.2% in 2026, versus 16.7% over the full period. It compares per-channel fees across both parties with the broadcaster's locked balance, excluding pending-payment amounts. The calculation illustrates how the wait can outweigh fees in a low-fee environment; it does not assume that operators earned that return.

The same distinction between fees and accessible funds matters for BOLT 3's zero-fee commitment design, which changes how miners are paid. A child transaction supplies the commitment's mining fee through child-pays-for-parent. Transactions resolving conditional pending payments, known as HTLCs, obtain fees through added inputs.

The broadcaster's delayed balance remains part of that design. Removing a fee from the pre-signed transaction therefore leaves both a paid settlement path and a waiting period to account for.

The measurements also have boundaries. Private cooperative closes are absent, splices are excluded from the close counts, and simple-taproot delays, HTLC resolutions and fee bumps are unclassified in the cost analysis. Confirmed-chain records cannot show failed or replaced fee bumps.

The released repository contains code and aggregate outputs, while underlying scan tables, channel lists and gossip snapshots are available from the author on request. For operators, the findings make access to funds part of the exit bill, alongside the transactions needed to recover them. Readers comparing wallet support for everyday Lightning payments can consult CryptoSlate’s Bitcoin wallet guide.

According to CoinGlass, the cumulative volume delta (CVD) on the Coinbase spot market reached -$1.08 billion between Oct. 31 and Nov. 15. CVD shows the difference between the volume of market buy orders and market sell orders, and a negative CVD means that sellers were more active on the exchange.

Over the same period, the CVD on the spot markets of OKX, Bybit and Binance stood at $240.3 million, $65.17 million and $51.88 million, respectively, so buyers were more active on these three exchanges.

The price of Bitcoin went down from $81,188 on Nov. 4 to $61,956 on Nov. 14, according to CoinGlass data, and the decline amounted to around 24%. On Sunday, Bitcoin recovered to around $65,400.

The data comes amid claims that Binance has been pushing the price of Bitcoin down. The exchange lost $6.4 billion in a hack on Oct. 29, and some users on X then claimed that Binance was selling crypto to cover its losses. Two weeks after the attack, Binance published a Proof of Reserves report that showed client balances on the exchange were fully backed.

This week, Binance founder Changpeng Zhao shared a comparison of Bitcoin charts ahead of the SpaceX and Anthropic IPOs and called it "an interesting analysis." Several users in the replies to his post blamed the drop in Bitcoin on selling by Binance.

Binance is the largest crypto exchange by trading volume, and a large share of futures liquidations takes place on the platform. On Nov. 13, crypto exchanges liquidated 187,389 traders for a total of $1.65 billion in 24 hours, and 88% of that amount came from long positions, according to CoinGlass. Still, the CVD on the Binance spot market has stayed positive since Oct. 31.

#5075. XRP Backer Counters SWIFT’s New Speed Report

Home » Ripple (XRP) » XRP Backer Counters SWIFT’s New Speed Report

The preference for nearly-immediate settlement time windows unites a roster of banks in SWIFT’s chain trial.

A Swift report highlighting faster cross-border payments drew a pointed response from Digital Asset Investor, who replied that he prefers 3-4 seconds and pointed to XRP.

The exchange underscores the ongoing contrast between improvements in traditional interbank messaging and the settlement times associated with blockchain-based rails.

Swift’s Spotlight on Speed report, released this week, shows that 50% of payments on its network now reach the recipient institution within 40 seconds, with 75% arriving within 10 minutes.

What will define the next generation of cross-border payments?The answer? More than just speed.Throughout @Sibos, conversations repeatedly focused on the customer experience. How do we make cross-border transactions more intuitive, more transparent and more predictable for… pic.twitter.com/yZoeZMDN4z

The cooperative noted that these figures put the industry ahead of the G20’s target for one-hour end-to-end processing by 2027 in the interbank leg of the journey.

The same report emphasizes that the “last mile”, the period after a payment reaches the receiving bank and before it is credited to the beneficiary’s account, still accounts for about 80% of the average end-to-end journey time.

Across 40 receiving markets analyzed, median last-mile processing sat near one hour in roughly one-third of cases, with wide variation between cross-border markets.

The conglomerate has called for greater use of one-leg-out models that connect international payments to domestic instant systems to reduce those final delays.

Digital Asset Investor’s reply to the Swift post was brief: “I prefer 3-4 seconds. XRP.” The comment references the XRP Ledger’s typical ledger close time of roughly 3-5 seconds, which provides finality for on-ledger transfers.

I prefer 3-4 seconds. XRP. https://t.co/tBqXtEsqeM

In Ripple’s On-Demand Liquidity (ODL) model, XRP is used as a bridge asset so that currency conversion and settlement can occur without pre-funded nostro accounts.

End-to-end ODL flows that include exchange conversions have been described in the 3-5 second range for the core ledger step, though real-world completion including compliance and local payouts is often measured in seconds to a few minutes depending on the corridor.

The two claims are not measuring identical segments of a payment. Swift’s 40-second figure tracks time to the recipient institution, while the longer last-mile delays occur after that point.

https://t.co/ZA3CcggMOf @swiftcommunity @XRP @realfrandeolza @Archie_XRPL

XRP’s cited 3-4 second window refers primarily to ledger settlement of the bridge asset itself.

Traditional systems still handle the bulk of global bank-to-bank volume and benefit from established compliance and messaging standards; blockchain rails emphasize reduced pre-funding and faster finality on the asset transfer.

Whether the shorter settlement window on XRP produces a meaningfully better end-user experience continues to depend on how the on- and off-ramps, local banking rails, and compliance steps are integrated in any given corridor.

#5074. Bitcoin ETFs Bleed $1.4B in Five Days as Investors Cut Risk

Bitcoin ETFs Bleed $1.4B in Five Days as Investors Cut Risk

U.S. spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds have recorded five consecutive days of net outflows, as investors retreat from risk assets after a turbulent week for markets.

The funds lost some $1.44 billion between November 5 and November 11, including $299.9 million on Wednesday, according to SoSoValue data. That brings net outflows for November so far to $1.88 billion, after $520 million left the funds in October.

The outflows have coincided with a sell-off in AI and technology stocks. On November 5, when the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.5% in a single day, Bitcoin ETFs saw net outflows of about $430 million.

"This wave of outflows is the result of institutional investors actively or passively reducing their risk exposure following a decline in macro risk appetite, which is not yet sufficient to prove that Bitcoin's long-term allocation thesis has reversed," Tim Sun, senior researcher at HashKey, told Decrypt.

The five-day outflows amount to about 2.6% of the funds' $55.1 billion in cumulative net inflows, "far from a full-scale retreat," Sun said. But the funds' total net assets have fallen to $93.7 billion, down about 45% from a peak of $169.5 billion in October 2025, as both outflows and falling prices take their toll.

Bitcoin is trading at $73,358, down 0.87% over the past 24 hours, according to Decrypt data. On Decrypt Predict, users put a 40% chance on Bitcoin trading above $74,000 on Sunday afternoon, and a 94% chance that it will hold above $70,000. Sun estimated that the average holding cost for spot Bitcoin ETFs is around $81,000, meaning some ETF holders are now sitting on unrealized losses, and that some investors may cut their exposure further as they reassess their allocations at year-end.

Analysts say the bigger concern is a shortage of new buyers. In a note shared with Decrypt, Greg Cipolaro, head of research at BitGo, said the post-election bounce brought only $75 million into spot Bitcoin ETFs, while the supply of dollar-pegged stablecoins contracted 1.9% to $286.3 billion, "suggesting little fresh capital is waiting on the sidelines." Onchain analytics firm Glassnode found that total stablecoin supply fell by $14.2 billion in the 30 days through November 9, the fastest contraction since June 2022, Decrypt reported on Wednesday.

The basis trade, in which hedge funds bought spot ETF shares while shorting futures to capture the price gap, has also become less attractive because the basis has fallen below borrowing costs, prompting many funds to exit, Cipolaro said. That means ETF flows may now reflect directional demand for Bitcoin more directly than before, according to Sun.

Corporate buyers have also slowed. The premium of Strategy's stock over the value of its Bitcoin holdings has narrowed, making it less attractive for the company to raise capital to buy more, while MSCI's decision to exclude it from its indexes could cut off passive investment, Sun said.

"The most critical factor to watch right now is the persistent lack of buying demand itself, the impact of which on prices may be more significant than the outflow figures alone," he said.

Cipolaro said Bitcoin had fallen with risk assets but lagged their recoveries. "Unless it begins to participate in rallies and ETF demand strengthens, digital assets could remain exposed to further downside without benefiting from a broader risk asset rebound," he wrote.

Many people forget just how long the 'winter' was for $GLD. It had an initial burst, even becaming the biggest ETF in world for one day in 2011 ,and then the bad times came and and it (saw 40% of investors bail) and took nearly a DECADE to get back to its that aum high again.… pic.twitter.com/Ny9gyyo1Am

"Assets without cash flows run purely on sentiment and it changes," he wrote.

#5073. Solana’s “retired” validators still vote with 15% of active stake

CryptoSlate matched 31 validators marked retired from the program to active vote accounts. Two accounted for just over half of the cohort’s stake.

Thirty-one Solana validators marked “Retired” by the Solana Foundation’s delegation program were still voting in a Nov. 14 snapshot. They carried 63 million SOL in delegated stake, about 15% of active stake in the voting accounts CryptoSlate examined.

The finding sharpens the question facing smaller validators under the Foundation’s published 12-month membership model: whether they can replace program support with other delegation.

CryptoSlate compared the Foundation’s participant register with voting data from Solana’s mainnet RPC endpoint, captured at approximately 05:15 UTC on November 14, 2026. The accompanying epoch response placed the observation at epoch 1086.

CryptoSlate identified 31 retired-program validators in current vote accounts with active stake. They carried 63 million SOL of the 429 million SOL across 663 such accounts, or 14.8% using the unrounded amounts.

Those SOL totals describe stake delegated to the voting accounts, rather than the validators’ beneficial ownership of the tokens. The denominator is the selected current voting set, rather than SOL’s circulating supply or the Foundation’s own stake.

The result establishes participation at the observation time. It does not establish that these validators retired under the current membership rules, or that the published membership rules caused their continued operation.

The Foundation’s delegation FAQ defines retirement as the end of membership in the Solana Foundation Delegation Program, or SFDP, and says retired validators no longer receive its stake delegations. It also says retirement is not a penalty or performance violation, and validators may continue operating on the permissionless network.

The FAQ describes a 12-month term measured from the first epoch a validator was eligible for a Foundation delegation on mainnet. It also specifies retirement when stake from outside SFDP exceeds 300,000 SOL and offers retiring or retired members an application route for renewal.

The Foundation publishes two different thresholds. Its delegation criteria still say a validator retires above 1 million SOL in outside stake, while the FAQ says 300,000 SOL. The criteria’s current mainnet table is labeled epoch 1084; neither page resolves which cutoff the Foundation applies in practice.

Program status, eligibility and actual funding also need to remain distinct. Approved onboarding makes a validator eligible for support, while performance requirements govern delegation and stake can take epochs to become active. Membership status alone therefore cannot identify how much Foundation stake an individual validator received.

The active retired cohort is concentrated: its two largest identities accounted for 52.5% of the cohort’s stake. Fourteen of the 31 identities had less than 300,000 SOL of total activated stake. That is a different measure from the FAQ’s external-stake threshold, and neither figure establishes profitability.

#5070. India's Financial Crimes Agency Searches CoinDCX, Delta Exchange Over Offshore Trades

India's Financial Crimes Agency Searches CoinDCX, Delta Exchange Over Offshore Trades

India's Enforcement Directorate has searched three premises in Bengaluru linked to crypto exchanges CoinDCX and Delta Exchange, alleging the platforms carried out unauthorized cross-border transactions worth hundreds of millions of dollars through crypto derivatives and tokenized assets.

The searches were carried out on November 4 and 5 under India's Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), the agency, India's main financial crimes investigator, said in a statement dated November 6, which it shared on X on Thursday.

ईडी, बेंगलुरु ने क्रिप्टो टोकन डेरिवेटिव एवं वास्तविक विश्व परिसंपत्ति (आरडब्ल्यूए) टोकन से जुड़े बड़े पैमाने पर अनधिकृत सीमा-पार वित्तीय लेन-देन के मामले में फेमा, 1999 के अंतर्गत मेसर्स नेब्लियो टेक्नोलॉजीज प्राइवेट लिमिटेड (“कॉइनडीसीएक्स”) तथा मेसर्स एक्सेलियम टेक्नोलॉजीज… pic.twitter.com/vXwMU5uCTj

The investigation targets Neblio Technologies, which operates CoinDCX, and Excelium Technologies, which runs Delta Exchange. Both platforms offered futures and options on crypto tokens and openly advertised trading in tokenized shares of foreign companies, despite not being authorized to do so, according to the agency.

The Enforcement Directorate alleged that CoinDCX used stablecoins such as USDT to carry out trades for its users on foreign crypto exchanges, including Binance, KuCoin, Bybit and Gate.io, bypassing India's framework for sending money abroad.

When users deposited rupees and placed spot or derivatives orders, CoinDCX converted the funds into USDT and opened matching positions on the foreign exchanges, the agency said. The trades ran through accounts held in the name of a Costa Rica-based group entity, which it described as a shell entity, and were carried out directly from CoinDCX through APIs.

Trades in tokenized shares of companies such as Apple, Google and Tesla were in fact derivatives positions opened on decentralized exchange Hyperliquid, according to the agency.

The Enforcement Directorate alleged that the cross-border transactions in each of these areas ran to hundreds of millions of dollars. It also said CoinDCX holds crypto assets in enterprise accounts on foreign exchanges, and has paid tens of millions of dollars in fees to those platforms in USDT, in breach of FEMA.

The agency said a large share of Delta Exchange's derivatives trading was executed through CoinDCX, and that Delta Exchange had transferred tens of millions of dollars to its overseas group entities, which is under investigation. Their fintech products also appear to contravene India's securities and central banking laws, it said, adding that its investigation is ongoing.

CoinDCX said in a tweet on November 6 that Enforcement Directorate officials had visited its Bengaluru office "as part of a routine enquiry" on November 4, and that it had fully cooperated. The exchange said it operates "in strict compliance with all applicable Indian laws, including FEMA," and adheres to its KYC, anti-money laundering and reporting obligations as an entity registered with India's Financial Intelligence Unit. Trading, deposits and withdrawals on the platform remain fully operational, it added.

Officials from the Enforcement Directorate visited our Bengaluru office as part of a routine enquiry on 4th November. We fully cooperated with the authorities and provided all necessary information and assistance.

As an entity registered with FIU-IND, we regularly…

Delta Exchange said in its own tweet on November 6 that it had cooperated fully with officials, and that its business "does not involve any cross-border transfer of VDAs in any form or manner," using India's term for crypto assets. It said it runs a dedicated rupee-settled exchange for Indian users only, has been registered with India's Financial Intelligence Unit since 2023, and that trading, deposits and withdrawals were functioning normally.

The investigation adds to a difficult stretch for CoinDCX, one of India's largest crypto exchanges. Last month, it confirmed a $16 million loss from retired wallets, days after co-founder and CEO Sumit Gupta called reports of a breach a "false alarm." That followed a roughly $44 million exploit in July 2025.

Coinbase, which has invested in CoinDCX since 2020, won approval from India's competition regulator to increase its minority stake in the exchange's parent company.

#5068. AI helped hackers gain access at 10 unnamed organizations, researchers say

The November 12 investigation reports 25 operations against at least 19 organizations during August–September, with humans assigning targets and able to steer.

AI-assisted attacks accessed systems or retrieved data at 10 organizations, according to a November 12 investigation by Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42. The security research team tracked 25 operations against at least 19 organizations during August and September 2026, including semiconductor companies, defense and policy organizations, and civil-society groups.

Unit 42 said the attackers used a customized version of Cairn, an open-source framework for AI-driven penetration testing, paired with Zhipu GLM and DeepSeek models.

The reported outcomes went beyond reconnaissance. The researchers reported unauthorized access to a semiconductor company's production system and to more than one million member records at a US teachers' union.

Attackers also modified a live standards-ballot document and obtained nonpublic data at an industry standards organization, the researchers said.

Humans supplied targets and goals, sometimes adding intelligence gathered beforehand. The framework then planned, executed and recorded subsequent work.

Individual operations lasted from 20 minutes to more than 50 hours, Unit 42 reported, with human steering still possible.

Activity: August–September 2026. Report: November 12, 2026. Unit 42 describes human-directed AI intrusions with continued steering possible.

Humans chose targets and could keep steering while agents repeated the intrusion work.

#5067. Digital Credit: Comparing The Six Bitcoin Preferred Stocks

A simple four-part investor framework for evaluating Digital Credit.

Digital credit is an emerging asset class that transforms corporate Bitcoin balance sheets into income producing securities. Strategy pioneered the market with five perpetual preferred equity instruments: STRK, STRF, STRD, STRC, and STRE (the first four are listed in the U.S.). Strive subsequently introduced SATA and SATS, bringing the category to six U.S. instruments across two issuers.

These securities offer investors preferred equity (read: credit-like) exposure to companies whose balance sheets are dominated by Bitcoin. Their perpetual structure means investors principally rely on recurring dividends and the continued financial strength of the issuer. Unlike term debt, there is no maturation date at which the full principal is ever paid back.

Evaluating digital credit requires examining four characteristics: creditworthiness, investor protections, liquidity, and dividend profile.

This article explains all four dimensions and then offers a ranking for the six digital credit instruments along these lines. None of this should be taken as investment advice—it is only a systematic framework for analyzing digital credit.

Creditworthiness measures an issuer’s ability to support its financial obligations.

Traditional credit analysis focuses on earnings, free cash flow, and refinancing capacity. Companies with strong cash generation can service interest and repay maturing debt. Digital credit issuers today derive financial strength primarily from their Bitcoin reserves, placing greater emphasis on net asset coverage. In the future we could certainly see digital credit issuers that also have significant cash flows on top of Bitcoin holdings, which would add to creditworthiness.

The central question is how much Bitcoin supports each dollar of credit obligations. One useful measure is the BTC Rating, which compares the dollar value of Bitcoin reserves with the outstanding credit, accounting for the seniority of each credit instrument. Cash reserves can further strengthen creditworthiness by reducing net obligations.

For example, a 5x BTC Rating indicates five dollars of Bitcoin supporting every dollar of notional credit claims. Higher ratings provide greater protection against Bitcoin price declines.

Seniority matters because instruments from the same issuer can have different claims on the same asset base. A senior preferred instrument benefits from greater coverage than a junior preferred instrument: all senior claims are included in the BTC Rating calculation of a junior instrument.

Creditworthiness also depends on corporate governance and capital allocation. Management must preserve sufficient Bitcoin coverage while funding recurring dividends. Issuing additional credit increases dividend obligations, while assets accumulation (Bitcoin or cash) strengthen the asset base. Excessive leverage, poor treasury management, or sustained Bitcoin declines can weaken coverage over time.

Investors must therefore evaluate both their assumptions about Bitcoin’s long term performance and management’s ability to maintain a sustainable capital structure.

Investor protections determine what happens when an issuer fails to pay its promised dividends.

While creditworthiness concerns an issuer’s ability to pay, investor protections govern the consequences of missed payments, and more specifically the compensation investors may receive for delayed income.

The first distinction is cumulative versus noncumulative dividends. Cumulative dividends continue accumulating when payments are skipped, preserving the investor’s claim to unpaid distributions. Noncumulative dividends permit the issuer to permanently forgo a payment.

The second distinction is the treatment of unpaid dividends. Some instruments preserve unpaid amounts without additional compensation. Others compound arrears at the regular dividend rate. The strongest protections impose penalty rates, which cause unpaid dividends to compound at progressively higher rates as deferrals continue.

Penalty rates create financial incentives for management to maintain regular payments. They also compensate investors for the additional risk and delay associated with missed distributions.

Other investor protections may include restrictions on payments to junior shareholders, preferred shareholder voting rights or director elections, and dedicated dividend reserves.

These provisions establish the contractual guardrails surrounding dividend payments. Stronger protections increase the cost of deferral and improve the investor’s position to receive income.

Liquidity measures how easily investors can enter and exit positions without materially affecting market prices. This is especially important for digital credit, which does not mature and pay back principal on a fixed date. A liquid market is how an investor would “get his money back” if he wants to exit his position.

Digital credit has developed substantial secondary market liquidity, particularly in its leading instruments. The six U.S.-listed digital credit tickers are among the most actively traded preferred equity securities in the U.S. markets.

Two metrics help investors evaluate liquidity.

Absolute trading volume measures the total dollar value traded over a given period. Greater volume accommodates larger transactions and makes it easier for institutions to establish or liquidate positions.

Relative liquidity, or turnover, measures trading volume as a percentage of an instrument’s market capitalization. It captures how actively a security trades relative to its outstanding size.

For example, an instrument with $50 million in daily volume and a $1 billion market capitalization has 5% daily turnover. Another instrument trading $100 million daily with a $10 billion market capitalization has only 1% turnover. The second instrument offers greater absolute trading capacity, while the first experiences substantially greater trading activity relative to its size.

Absolute volume facilitates large transactions, while relative turnover reveals the level of trading activity relative to the capital outstanding.

Dividend profile describes the characteristics of the income an investor receives. Three main considerations are the dividend rate policy, payment frequency, and dividend yield.

The first distinction is between fixed and variable dividends. Fixed dividends establish a predetermined annual payment per share. Investors know the nominal income they are entitled to receive, allowing them to plan around a predictable cash flow stream. Variable dividends allow issuers to adjust the payout rate over time. These adjustments can respond to market interest rates, investor demand, or the trading price of the instrument. Fixed dividends prioritize income predictability for investors with reduced flexibility for issuers. Variable dividends provide flexibility for issuers but less predictability for investors.

The second consideration is payment frequency. Traditional preferred securities generally pay quarterly. Digital credit has introduced monthly, twice monthly, and daily dividend schedules. More frequent payments improve cash flow availability, accelerate reinvestment opportunities, and reduce the concentration of distributions around individual payment dates. After January 1 2027, all six instruments will be doing daily dividends.

The third consideration, and perhaps the most important out of anything mentioned in this article, is the raw dividend yield. This is the annualized income received divided by the trading price of the credit. A higher yield is generally preferred, but it also must be contextualized against risks and other considerations.

The following framework ranks the six instruments relative to one another. Rank 1 represents the strongest position and rank 6 the weakest, with ties where instruments share identical characteristics.

Creditworthiness and investor protections receive overall rankings. Liquidity is segmented into absolute trading volume and turnover. Dividend profile is segmented into rate certainty and yield. While each category’s segments can be evaluated together as a composite metric based on the investor’s own needs, I am choosing to segment them for more precision. I have also thrown out payment frequency since all six will be daily in less than two months.

For dividend rate certainty, fixed dividends rank ahead of variable dividends because their nominal payments are predetermined. This ranking specifically measures income predictability.

Equal signs indicate tied rankings. Liquidity rankings are based on average daily trading volumes from November 2–11, 2026, and turnover is calculated using the latest reported shares outstanding.

Creditworthiness: Strategy’s preferreds rank ahead of Strive’s because of their greater asset coverage. Within each issuer, seniority determines the ranking. STRF has the highest BTC Rating because it is Strategy’s most senior preferred, while SATS has the lowest coverage because it ranks below SATA in Strive’s capital structure.

Investor protections: SATA and STRF rank first and second because unpaid dividends compound at escalating penalty rates and holders can elect directors following prolonged dividend deferrals. SATA’s higher penalty rate ceiling and dividend reserve give it the edge. STRC and STRK both compound unpaid dividends at the regular dividend rate. I rank STRC ahead of STRK based on its higher current compounding rate, although STRK also gives holders the right to elect directors after prolonged dividend deferrals. SATS has cumulative dividends, but unpaid dividends do not compound. STRD ranks last because its dividends are noncumulative, meaning any skipped dividends are permanently forgone. Investors also have no right to bring on directors.

Of the six, STRC and SATA are variable rate instruments and the remaining four are fixed rate. This makes the dividend rate policy pretty straightforward.

The remaining columns—volume, turnover, and yield—are trackable numbers. For instance, here are turnover and volume numbers from the BFC Digital Credit Dashboard:

Each of the six digital credit instruments has a different set of tradeoffs. Investors who prioritize creditworthiness may prefer STRF, while those who prioritize dividend certainty and yield may prefer SATS.

The relative importance of each of these dimensions depends on the investor’s own needs. As digital credit continues to develop, investors can use this framework to evaluate new instruments and determine which ones are best suited to their objectives.

#5064. Morning Minute: Tokenized Stock Venues Are Launching Without Big Tech’s Approval

Morning Minute: Tokenized Stock Venues Are Launching Without Big Tech’s Approval

Morning Minute is a daily newsletter written by Tyler Warner. The analysis and opinions expressed are his own and do not necessarily reflect those of Decrypt. And check out our daily news show 'FOMO HOUR' covering all of the top stories and market action.

🏛️ OKX’s Tokenized Stock Venue Launches Without Big Tech

In September, after the CLARITY Act died in the Senate, the SEC created an innovation exemption letting venues trade tokenized versions of US stocks without waiting for new legislation. It came with one condition. A company that doesn’t want a third party minting tokens of its shares can object in writing within 30 days, and that’s the end of it.

Companies have been objecting ever since. The count at the OKXICE venue went from 22 in October to 50, then 56, and as of its November 5 notice, 67. Every member of the Magnificent Seven is on that list.

OKXICE is launching anyway, on November 23. The venue will list more than 70 assets, though 59 of them are Direxion ETFs. The individual stocks that made it through are Coinbase, Circle, Robinhood, Strategy, BitGo, Securitize and Better.com. Strategy is also tokenizing its preferred shares.

Securitize handles the tokenization, each token is backed one-for-one by a real share and carries dividends and voting rights, and trading runs through Uniswap v4 pools on X Layer, OKX’s Ethereum layer-2.

So a venture between a global exchange and the parent of the New York Stock Exchange built a tokenized equities market, and what it opens with is seven crypto companies and a series of leveraged ETFs.

Notably, this news comes just a day after the NYSE picked Avalanche to handle clearing and settlement for its own 24/7 tokenized securities platform, with a fourth-quarter target for launch after about a year of testing. The NYSE has signed agreements with Broadridge, Computershare, Equiniti and Superstate to support issuer-sponsored tokenized securities and transfer-agent functions. When the company’s own share registry issues the token, there is nothing to veto.

DTCC is doing a version of this too, with a tokenization service that went live October 28 on the Canton Network carrying 20 participants including Bank of America, Citi, JPMorgan and Citadel Securities. Morgan Stanley has already run equities and Treasuries through it.

Progress is being made, slowly but surely. It just gets built slowly, through transfer agents and clearing houses, by the incumbents. Now we wait to see how the market reacts to these first launches…

#5062. Bitcoin Price Briefly Crashes to $67,500, Lowest Since August, as Dollar Holds 19-Month High

Bitcoin price traded near $69,800 on Friday morning after briefly crashing to about $67,555 around midnight Eastern, its lowest level since mid-August, according to Bitcoin Magazine Pro data. The rebound held after October producer prices rose less than economists had expected, though the U.S. dollar remained near a 19-month high and traders still fully priced a December Federal Reserve rate hike.

Bitcoin price was trading near $72,800 at this time Thursday. It slipped toward $71,000 by Thursday evening, then gave way late at night, breaking below $70,000 and sliding to that midnight low. The move also pushed the bitcoin price below its 200-week moving average, a long-term trend line near $68,000. Buyers lifted it back above $69,000 before sunrise, and the rebound extended toward $69,800 after the producer-price report.

The U.S. Dollar Index held above 103 Friday after a three-day rally took it to its highest level since April 2025. The 10-year Treasury yield was near 5.15% ahead of the data, and two-year yields, which track Fed expectations most closely, were on pace for their worst week since 2024, Bloomberg reported.

Traders still see an 88% chance of a quarter-point hike at the Fed’s Dec. 8-9 meeting and a 12% chance of a half-point move, CME FedWatch data show. Fed Governor Christopher Waller has added a 50-basis-point increase to the discussion, and New York Fed President John Williams said Thursday that inflation remains high and policymakers need to take further action.

Higher rates raise the cost of holding an asset that pays no interest, and a stronger dollar tends to drain demand for risk assets. Both have pressured the bitcoin price since this week’s hotter-than-expected consumer price index.

Bitcoin has also broken from tech stocks. It fell 5.9% between Nov. 5 and Nov. 12 while the Nasdaq 100 gained 6.4%, a sign it is trading more on yields and the dollar than on the AI trade. Nasdaq 100 futures were up about 0.6% Friday after the producer-price report, as investors also weighed Nvidia’s announcement that Jensen Huang had resigned as CEO.

The break below $70,000 set off a wave of forced selling. About $1.64 billion in crypto positions were liquidated over 24 hours, with bets on higher prices making up nearly 89% of the total and bitcoin positions accounting for $916 million.

U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs added to the pressure. The funds posted about $47.7 million in net outflows Thursday, their sixth straight day of withdrawals, bringing the run to roughly $1.49 billion. BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) alone bled about $2 billion over nine sessions through Wednesday, and the group has now flipped to about $1.56 billion in net outflows for 2026.

Sentiment has soured with it. A widely watched crypto fear and greed gauge dropped to 20 Friday, its lowest reading since July 8, and bitcoin is now on track for a second straight down year.

Positioning has turned defensive. Average perpetual futures funding rates turned negative for the first time in a month as the price fell toward $68,500, meaning short sellers are now paying to hold their bets. Order books are also thin. Bitcoin order-book depth across major exchanges fell to $72 million on Nov. 9, roughly 33% below normal levels. “Liquidity remains thin while leverage stays elevated, leaving the market vulnerable to sharp moves in either direction,” said Tanay Ved, a senior research associate at Talos.

The Labor Department said Friday that the Producer Price Index for final demand rose 0.3% in October, short of the 0.4% monthly increase economists had expected, after a revised 1.4% advance in September. Core prices, which exclude food and energy, increased 0.3%, matching forecasts. On an unadjusted basis, the headline index was up 6.5% from a year earlier, the largest 12-month rise since November 2022. The slightly cooler report took some pressure off the dollar, which still held above 103, but a December rate hike remains fully priced, leaving limited relief for the bitcoin price heading into the weekend.

At the time of writing, the bitcoin price is near $69,800.

#5061. AI models agreed with each other more than with reality in a new test

Science Prediction Universe found that pooling rankings improved average results, while shared scientific errors survived.

AI models agreed more closely with one another than with laboratory measurements in a new test of AI predictions. Pooling their rankings improved results on average, but several systems could still share the same mistake.

The Science Prediction Universe study, led by UniPat AI and submitted to arXiv on Nov. 11, tested 13 agent configurations spanning 12 models on 100 public tasks and 16 private tasks. Each configuration combined a model, reasoning setting and agent software. The study asked them to rank specified experiments across chemistry, materials science, biology and medicine.

Science Prediction Universe researchers reported that, on the public tasks, average agreement between scored configurations reached a Spearman rank correlation of 0.52, compared with 0.33 against measured outcomes. Agreement between agents exceeded their correlation with measurements on 81 of the 100 tasks. These averages use available scored predictions, with coverage varying by configuration.

Those figures describe how closely orderings match, rather than percentages of answers correct. Agents might rank reaction conditions by yield or materials by conductivity without having to predict numerical values. A perfect ordering without measurement ties scores 1; random rankings average 0.

The researchers found a benefit to pooling predictions. Averaging each experiment's position across configurations produced a consensus ranking that scored 0.08 points above the average submission, improving results on 73 of the 100 public tasks. The reported 95% confidence interval for the gain was 0.05 to 0.11.

On one oncology task, eleven configurations agreed at 0.9 but averaged just 0.27 against measurements. The benchmark’s best individual system also beat the consensus of its peers on matched tasks.

More broadly, tasks with greater agreement tended to have better predictions. The paper's agreement analysis therefore presents consensus as an informative but fallible signal. The authors explain that averaging can reduce errors that differ between systems while retaining common ones.

Pooling rankings improved average predictions in SPU. Comparing the public-task average with one oncology task shows why agreement still needs an experimental check.

Mean pairwise agreement was 0.52, while the mean score against measurements was 0.33, using available scored predictions.

Eleven configurations agreed strongly on one oncology task, but their rankings matched the measurements much less closely.

Agreement contains useful signal, but shared errors can survive a consensus.

Available scored predictions have unequal configuration coverage. The average covers 100 public tasks; the oncology view is one task with eleven configurations. Correlations are not percentages correct. Neither view measures human scientific ability.

Reported public-task agreement and measurement correlations share a -1 to 1 axis. Dot x = left + (correlation + 1) / 2 × axis width. Pooling paths are labelled schematic. Consensus gain is 0.081 score points (95% CI 0.054 to 0.110), higher on 73/100 public tasks.

Available scored predictions have unequal configuration coverage. The average covers 100 public tasks; the oncology view is one task with eleven configurations. Correlations are not percentages correct. Neither view measures human scientific ability.

The authors connect those shared errors to simple assumptions about how experimental outcomes should rise or fall. If several agents rely on the same mistaken relationship, collecting more of their opinions can preserve that error.

The configurations were scored on different task sets. Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1 had scores on only 44 and 30 public tasks, respectively, largely because of safety refusals. Across the full benchmark, all 13 configurations shared just 28 scored tasks: 27 public and one private.

The public tasks also looked backward at published measurements and were selected after pilot evaluations. The private set contained only 16 tasks across four unpublished experimental series, limiting how broadly its findings can be applied.

There was useful predictive ability in that private set: twelve of the 13 configurations ranked the unpublished experiments significantly better than chance overall, according to UniPat's Nov. 12 results release. Of 208 official private runs, 159 were scored.

The study used no human prediction baseline. Its findings apply to ranking the experimental outcomes it tested, with lab measurements still needed to check the answers.

#5060. DTCC to Bring Tokenized Stocks and Treasuries to Solana in 2027

DTCC to Bring Tokenized Stocks and Treasuries to Solana in 2027

The Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation (DTCC), the backbone of U.S. securities settlement, plans to bring its tokenized securities to Solana, it announced on Thursday.

The firm will connect the DTCC Tokenization Service (DTS) to the Solana network, allowing eligible assets held by its Depository Trust Company (DTC) subsidiary to be converted into tokens on Solana. The integration is planned for the second half of 2027.

BREAKING: @The_DTCC to tokenize custodied assets on Solana. announced plans to connect the DTCC Tokenization Service to Solana, enabling the tokenization of eligible DTC-custodied assets on the network.

The integration is planned for the second half of 2027, further advancing… pic.twitter.com/gXszWFgUOX

"DTCC is bringing regulated, DTC-tokenized securities to another major blockchain ecosystem, giving market participants greater choice in where they access and utilize tokenized assets," DTCC CEO Frank La Salla said.

DTS went live on October 28 on the Canton Network and DTCC's own private blockchain, built on the Besu framework, with more networks due to be added in 2027, according to DTCC's launch announcement. The service creates tokenized "digital twins" of securities held at DTC, which custodies more than $114 trillion in assets. Solana joins Stellar and Circle's Arc blockchain, which are expected to be added in 2027, according to a DTCC fact sheet.

Under a no-action letter from the SEC, the service is limited to a defined set of highly liquid assets, including Russell 1000 stocks, ETFs tracking major indexes, and U.S. Treasuries. Morgan Stanley said last week it had tokenized U.S. stocks and Treasuries through the service.

Tokens issued on Solana "will retain the same investor protections, ownership rights and regulatory safeguards that apply to traditionally held securities," said Brian Steele, president of DTCC Clearing & Securities Services.

Solana has been actively courting traditional finance in recent months, with Solana Foundation head of institutional Nick Ducoff arguing that, "Institutions choose Solana because it already runs real financial activity at scale." He added that institutions are "already issuing, settling and deploying capital" on the network, in a tweet shared by Solana's official account.

Last month, the Solana Foundation unveiled an open standard for institutional settlement developed with input from J.P. Morgan, and the network completed its Alpenglow upgrade, cutting the time it takes for transactions to become final to roughly 150 milliseconds.

Solana is also lining up more venues for tokenized stocks. Trading platform Formation has notified the SEC of plans to trade tokenized U.S. stocks on Solana, starting with Galaxy and Forward Industries.

#5058. President Trump Taps Two Democrats in Bipartisan Slate of SEC and CFTC Nominees as Both Agencies Run Short-Handed

President Donald Trump sent the Senate four nominees for the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission on Thursday, his first picks for either agency in about a year and the first Democrats he has put forward for them.

Former CFTC Commissioner Kristin Johnson, a Democrat, and Republican Steven Levine were nominated to the SEC. Republican Nathan Anonick and Democrat Matthew Rowland were nominated to the CFTC, Bloomberg Law reported.

Each nominee needs Senate confirmation. The Senate Banking Committee will handle the SEC picks, while the Senate Agriculture Committee will take up the CFTC pair before any vote by the full chamber.

Levine was tapped for the SEC seat left by Hester Peirce, whose term expired, for a term running through June 5, 2030. He most recently served as general counsel and a senior adviser at the White House Council of Economic Advisers and previously worked at the SEC as counsel and deputy chief of staff to Commissioner Mark Uyeda.

Peirce led the SEC’s Crypto Task Force and was one of the agency’s most vocal supporters of clearer crypto rules.

Johnson would take the seat formerly held by Democrat Caroline Crenshaw, for a term ending June 5, 2029. She served as a CFTC commissioner until 2025 and is a former law school professor. During her time at the CFTC, she spoke often about digital assets, including custody and decentralized finance.

Both CFTC nominees come from the Senate Agriculture Committee, which oversees the derivatives regulator. Anonick is legislative counsel to Chairman John Boozman and was a lead negotiator on the committee’s portion of the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act. He was nominated to the seat once held by former Chairman Rostin Behnam, for a term ending June 19, 2031.

Rowland is a CFTC attorney detailed to the committee who also worked on the Clarity Act and the committee’s 2024 crypto bill. He previously served on Johnson’s staff at the CFTC, according to his LinkedIn profile. He would fill the remainder of former Commissioner Summer Mersinger’s term, which expires April 13, 2028.

Both agencies can seat up to five commissioners, with no more than three from one party. The SEC currently has two, Chairman Paul Atkins and Commissioner Mark Uyeda. Chairman Mike Selig is the CFTC’s only sitting commissioner.

The timing puts the nominees in front of a Senate in its lame-duck session, weeks after Democrats swept both chambers of Congress in the Nov. 3 midterms. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, one of crypto’s sharpest critics, is expected to chair the Banking Committee when the new Congress is seated in January.

The pairing of Democrats with Republicans could matter for confirmation. After the election, TD Cowen’s Jaret Seiberg told clients he did not expect Democrats to confirm Trump nominees unless the president filled Democratic seats at agencies such as the SEC, a step he called unlikely. Thursday’s slate does exactly that at both regulators.

The nominations also land with crypto market structure legislation stalled. The Clarity Act failed a Senate cloture vote 49-50 on Sept. 15 and dies on Jan. 3 unless the lame-duck session revives it.

Without new law, the SEC and CFTC have set crypto policy largely on their own this year. Selig’s CFTC opened the door to equity perpetual futures, and a federal judge later said the agency likely overstepped while letting trading continue.

The White House did not say when it expects the Senate to act. The open question is whether a Senate heading for Democratic control moves the four nominees before January, or leaves the SEC and CFTC running with skeleton commissions into 2027.

#5057. Lido’s lending plan could block loan repayments without stopping interest

The lending plan distinguishes a limited freeze from a broader pause that blocks repayments and lender withdrawals. Interest for the paused period can still be added once accounting resumes.

Under Lido Lend’s proposed emergency rules, borrowers could be blocked from paying down debt and lenders from withdrawing. When the pause ends, borrowers could owe more: the next successful interest update would count the time they spent locked out.

The distinction appears in Lido Lend’s November 9 consolidated proposal. The proposed lending protocol, built on a modified version of Morpho Blue, uses a controller contract to permit or reject market actions. It separates a limited market freeze from a broader controller pause. Only the second shuts down repayment, liquidation and lender settlement together. Lenders supply loan tokens that borrowers take out against pledged collateral.

The proposal reports that the core contracts are deployed on Ethereum mainnet, but the DAO would have to accept the protocol separately. Each market would then need its own motion or DAO vote. The forum discussion continued with a signer declaration on November 14; the thread did not announce a completed acceptance vote or creation of the first market.

A Guardian ban stops an account’s new borrowing and collateral maturation but does not itself stop repayment, liquidation, settlement or collateral withdrawal under the remaining rules. The expected first WETH/wstETH market would launch with one contributor-run Guardian and a 1-of-1 quorum, with independent Guardians intended later.

Under the market controller rules, a freeze stops new borrowing, new collateral from completing its activation delay, and collateral withdrawals from positions carrying debt. Repayment, liquidation, lender withdrawals and settlement remain available, subject to their ordinary checks.

The Risk Steward Committee could impose that freeze and tighten defined controller settings through its dashboard, but could not loosen them. The proposed Operational Committee would use bounded Easy Track motions, open to LDO-holder objections, for actions such as unfreezing.

Borrowers can pay down debt, a key consideration when comparing crypto loan terms. Lenders can withdraw available loan tokens or use eligible settlement, which reduces a lender’s claim and a borrower’s debt by the same amount in exchange for collateral valued by the protocol’s price feed.

Settlement is the mechanism behind the Fallback Exits CryptoSlate examined in October. Lenders can exit without available loan tokens, but settlement is subject to market rules and policy limits. Bad debt at the front of the borrower queue can block it.

An Exit Book, a system for posting withdrawal requests, has a separate pause that stops new withdrawal requests and fills in that book. Owners can still cancel requests or use underlying positions directly, but those routes cannot bypass a paused market controller.

A pause blocks those routes. The architecture specification says it stops actions subject to the controller, including repayment, lender withdrawals, liquidation, settlement and direct interest updates. Even a direct call to the core cannot bypass the pause. Vault-share transfers and core functions outside the controller’s scope remain available.

Blocking an interest-update call does not make the borrowing period free. The core accounting specification uses elapsed time to calculate interest, and the controller rules explicitly say a later successful accrual covers time since the last update. A borrower could therefore regain repayment access with a larger debt balance under the applicable interest-rate model.

Proposed controls differ in scope. A controller pause closes repayment and lender exits while elapsed-time interest still counts.

For the banned account, new borrowing and collateral maturation stop. Repayment, liquidation and lender exits remain subject to normal rules.

New borrowing, collateral maturation and debt-bearing collateral withdrawal stop. Repayment, liquidation and lender exits remain available under normal rules.

Repayment, liquidation and lender withdrawal or settlement are blocked, alongside other controller-checked actions. The interest clock is not stopped.

New requests and fills stop in the book. Cancellation and direct core or vault access remain subject to the underlying market’s controls.

A finite emergency power does not guarantee a finite interruption: a separate Reseal path can make an active pause indefinite.

Proposed Lido Lend design, not a live pause. Available routes remain subject to normal rules and other active controls. Interest depends on the IRM. Live market settings and permissions are not independently verified.

Source-bound permission and authority diagrams from the November 9 proposal and current specifications. Arrows identify affected action routes, not quantities or guaranteed execution. No numerical outcome chart is warranted.

Proposed Lido Lend design, not a live pause. Available routes remain subject to normal rules and other active controls. Interest depends on the IRM. Live market settings and permissions are not independently verified.

There is a protective reason to suspend more than new borrowing. The proposal warns that initial price feeds, or oracles, use issuer-published collateral rates, which may diverge from secondary-market prices. If collateral falls in the market without a corresponding rate change, liquidation may become uneconomic and settlement may deliver collateral worth less than the debt canceled. Pausing those transactions can contain that risk, while also interrupting borrowers trying to repay.

The proposed Lend Emergency Brakes Committee has a 3-of-6 signing threshold. Through CircuitBreaker, it could trigger one fixed-duration controller pause per registration while maintaining required liveness signals, called heartbeats. It could not select the duration, extend the pause or end it early.

The roles specification assigns duration configuration and pauser registration to a separate administrator within immutable bounds. The committee’s successful pause consumes its registration, so another use requires re-registration.

The repository’s mainnet profile selects a configuration with an initial pause of five minutes and a permitted range from one minute to 60 days. The first market’s actual setting has not been confirmed.

Automatic expiry also has an exception. The proposal says the protocol-wide Reseal Manager can make a pause indefinite when Dual Governance is outside its normal state. The published Reseal Manager and Dual Governance implementations require an active finite pause and an authorized Reseal Committee acting through the governance contract. That path can replace the finite pause with an indefinite one without a fresh ordinary DAO vote at that step.

These controls apply per Lido Lend market and do not themselves move user assets. Separate DAO-controlled proxy upgrades remain part of the protocol’s trust assumptions.

For the first WETH/wstETH market, watch for the configured pause duration and who can extend it indefinitely. Those decisions will determine how long borrowers could be stuck with an interest bill they cannot stop by repaying.

#5056. SoFi Brings Its Bank-Issued Stablecoin to Polygon’s Payments Stack

SoFi Brings Its Bank-Issued Stablecoin to Polygon’s Payments Stack

SoFi is widening the reach of its digital dollar, bringing SoFiUSD, the first stablecoin issued by a U.S. national bank, onto Polygon’s payments infrastructure as banks and fintechs push stablecoins deeper into everyday money movement.

Polygon Labs said Thursday that SoFiUSD is now live on Polygon Open Money Stack, a payments layer that bundles fiat on- and off-ramps, embedded wallets and cross-chain settlement into a single integration.

The move adds Polygon alongside Ethereum and Solana, the networks SoFiUSD already runs on, and lets SoFi’s more than 17 million members buy, sell, hold, and convert the token on Polygon directly in the SoFi app, without opening a separate crypto wallet or manually bridging assets between chains.

“SoFi is well positioned to bring stablecoins into mainstream finance because it combines the regulatory foundation of a national bank with the reach of a major consumer and enterprise technology platform,” said Marc Boiron, CEO of Polygon Labs.

The expansion lands as stablecoins move beyond crypto trading into the plumbing used to settle card payments, pay businesses, and send money across borders.

On Polygon Open Money Stack, SoFiUSD joins USDC, USDT and PayPal’s PYUSD, and can connect to the wallets, banking rails, and local currencies businesses need for payouts, settlement and cross-border transfers, opening up uses well beyond consumer trading.

The token is redeemable one-to-one for U.S. dollars and issued by SoFi Bank, which is regulated by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency.

SoFi launched SoFiUSD late last year across Ethereum and Solana as the first stablecoin from a U.S. national bank, and it already settles the company’s entire card program over Mastercard’s network. The firm has been building out a broader digital-money suite, recently launching SoFi Earn, a tokenized deposit that pays 4.40% yield and converts one-to-one into SoFiUSD.

For Polygon, the addition deepens a payments business that has become one of the network’s calling cards.

Polygon recently extended Open Money Stack to Solana, and the chain has processed more than $3 trillion in lifetime stablecoin transfer volume, according to the company. Visa and Mastercard support stablecoin settlement on Polygon, while Stripe uses it to route USDC payments for merchants in more than 150 countries.

SoFiUSD is a payment stablecoin, not a bank deposit, and is not FDIC- or SIPC-insured, bank-guaranteed or legal tender.

#5052. Is Ethereum the “worst asset of all time,” amid estimated $8.83 billion BitMine loss ?

A dashboard shared by trader Flood estimates an unrealized loss of about $9 billion, but applies August purchase costs to November holdings.

Trader Flood, who posts as @ThinkingUSD, called Ethereum a “contender for the worst asset of all time” on Nov. 13, sharing a dashboard that put BitMine’s unrealized loss at about $9 billion.

The image marked the Ethereum treasury company 43% underwater. Its holdings match BitMine’s November disclosure, while its average-cost field is dated August. Applying that older average to the later balance approximately reproduces the dashboard’s displayed cost, leaving its loss figure dependent on that assumption.

Flood cited money lost to hacks, development time spent on inadequate tools and retail losses from betting on Ethereum’s price. He supplied no figures for those categories or comparative data establishing an all-time ranking. His criticism targeted Ethereum, with the BitMine dashboard providing a specific example of treasury exposure.

The image Flood shared listed 6,070,092 ETH, a $3,380 average cost, a $20.52 billion total cost basis and an $11.69 billion market value. Its displayed unrealized loss was $8,829,920,029.

The average-cost field is labeled as the filed average for Aug. 31, 2026. BitMine’s annual accounts reported 5,901,837 ETH at that date, with a cost basis of about $19.95 billion and a fair value of about $14.56 billion. Dividing the cost by the quantity gives approximately $3,380 per ETH.

Those accounts were filed on Nov. 10, but the holdings and cost figures describe the August balance.

BitMine’s Nov. 9 release reported a larger holding of 6,070,092 ETH as of Nov. 8 at 2 p.m. ET. Multiplying that quantity by the rounded August average produces roughly the $20.52 billion cost basis displayed on Flood’s dashboard.

That calculation extrapolates across two reporting dates. It reproduces the rounded total without confirming the dashboard’s underlying methodology or establishing what the expanded ETH holding actually cost. The November release supplies no updated aggregate cost basis.

The dashboard’s $8.83 billion loss estimate is therefore an unrealized mark against an assumed cost. It provides no evidence that BitMine sold those holdings and realized the loss in cash.

Lee’s position in the Nov. 9 company release remained bullish. BitMine’s chairman described ETH as trusted collateral and argued that tokenization and AI would support its role as a store of value.

The company also reported 5,227,037 staked ETH as of Nov. 8. That staking position is distinct from the market-price gap illustrated by the dashboard.

#5051. Jensen Huang Resigns as Nvidia CEO, With CFO Colette Kress Named Interim Chief

Jensen Huang Resigns as Nvidia CEO, With CFO Colette Kress Named Interim Chief

Jensen Huang has resigned as CEO of Nvidia, ending a 33-year tenure at the helm of the chipmaker he co-founded, after reports of affairs with a suspected Chinese spy and a senior company executive.

Huang has stepped down as president, CEO and a member of the board, effective immediately, Nvidia said on Thursday. Colette Kress, Nvidia's chief financial officer since 2013, will serve as interim CEO while remaining CFO, as the board searches for a permanent successor from both inside and outside the company. Nvidia did not give a reason for Huang's resignation, but thanked him for his "immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry."

NVIDIA announces CEO transition. Read the release: https://t.co/MTTUvFHCJA

— NVIDIA Newsroom (@nvidianewsroom) November 12, 2026

The board also named Harvey Jones, a former CEO and executive chairman of chip design software company Synopsys, as its first-ever chair.

"The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company's operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption," Jones said.

Kress said she was "committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years." Nvidia will report its third-quarter results as scheduled on Tuesday, the company said.

Nvidia shares were down 7.7% at $160.28 shortly after the market opened on Thursday, having fallen as low as $148.80, according to Yahoo! Finance data.

Huang's departure comes four days after he acknowledged in a letter to staff that he had been unfaithful to his wife, prompting Nvidia's board to open an independent investigation. He had told the board that he had been intimate with Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based Nvidia customer Megaspeed, The New York Times reported.

The Times had reported in October that U.S. officials had concluded Alice Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset, while the Financial Times later reported that a U.S. government memo said the two had been romantically involved. China has denied the allegations.

On Wednesday, the Times reported that Huang had also had a relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care, who reports to him. The Wall Street Journal later reported that the board was preparing to oust him, adding to the pressure on the CEO.

The scandal has wiped hundreds of billions of dollars off Nvidia's market value, with the company losing about $430 billion in two days earlier this week. Nvidia and Huang also face a proposed shareholder class action, and lawmakers had threatened to subpoena him.

Huang ran Nvidia with about 60 executives reporting directly to him and has said he did not believe in succession planning, leaving the company without an obvious successor.

Prior to the announcement of Huang's resignation, one person inside the company had told the Financial Times that naming Kress as interim CEO would be the simplest option. Other potential candidates cited by the paper's sources include Ian Buck, who runs Nvidia's data center business, and Arm CEO Rene Haas, a former Nvidia executive.

Huang remains Nvidia's largest shareholder, with a stake of about 3.6%, according to the Journal.

#5049. Robinhood’s Crypto Trading Volume Falls 48% in October as Event Contracts More Than Double

Crypto trading on Robinhood fell by almost half from a year ago in October, the company said Thursday, as customers traded $17 billion of digital assets while their bets on event contracts more than doubled.

The $17 billion figure was down 21% from September and 48% from October 2025, when crypto notional volume reached $32.5 billion. It covers both the flagship Robinhood app and Bitstamp, the crypto exchange the company bought in 2025.

Volume in the Robinhood app fell to $6.8 billion, down 24% from September and 51% from a year earlier. Bitstamp handled $10.2 billion, down 18% month over month and 45% year over year.

Average daily crypto volume across both platforms came to $548 million, compared with $713 million in September and about $1.05 billion a year ago. Daily average crypto trades slipped to about 700,000 from 900,000 in September and 1.1 million in October 2025.

The contrast with Robinhood’s prediction markets business is stark. Customers traded 5.9 billion event contracts in October, up 5% from September and 136% from the 2.5 billion traded a year earlier. Average daily volume reached 190 million contracts.

Robinhood counts crypto and prediction markets on the same 31-day calendar, since both trade every day, so the comparison is apples to apples. Event contracts let users bet on outcomes such as elections, sports and economic data, and October’s tally covered the final weeks before the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

That growth has drawn scrutiny in Washington. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, who is set to chair the Senate Banking Committee in January, plans to crack down on prediction markets and election betting platforms.

The rest of Robinhood’s brokerage held up better than crypto. Equity notional volume rose 2% from a year earlier to $325 billion, and options contracts traded climbed 8% to 289 million. Margin balances reached $22.9 billion, up 39% year over year.

Funded customers rose by about 130,000 in the month to 28.9 million, and net deposits came to $15.1 billion. Total platform assets slipped 3% from September to $383 billion but were up 12% from a year earlier.

Robinhood did not say why crypto activity fell. The release, like all of the company’s monthly updates, is unaudited and preliminary.

The slump in Robinhood’s crypto numbers lines up with a broader retreat by retail traders. Bitcoin ended September near $83,500 and has slid since, falling below $70,000 early Friday for the first time since August as a hot inflation report raised bets on a Federal Reserve rate hike in December.

Institutional demand has cooled alongside it. U.S. spot bitcoin exchange-traded funds posted a sixth straight day of net outflows on Thursday, and BlackRock’s IBIT, the largest of them, bled about $2 billion over nine sessions through Wednesday. Spot bitcoin ETFs have now erased their net inflows for 2026.

Crypto trading generates transaction revenue for Robinhood, so lower volume generally means fewer fees, even when assets on the platform keep growing. The company reports full fourth-quarter results early next year, and October’s figures are the first look at how the quarter started.

The company has kept expanding its crypto footprint anyway. In October, Robinhood won a license in Dubai to offer bitcoin and stock trading in the Middle East starting in 2027.

Robinhood also said cash and deposit balances fell 20% in October to $16.4 billion, mostly because customers were net buyers, and that the decline has largely reversed in early November. November’s operating data will show whether this month’s selloff below $70,000 brought crypto traders back or pushed more of them toward event contracts.

#5047. The Fed could rescue bond markets and still make life harder for Bitcoin

Lorie Logan wants emergency support for Treasury markets while favoring further rate hikes, leaving Bitcoin exposed to tighter monetary policy.

Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan proposed stronger tools to keep Treasury markets functioning during a crisis while leaving room for higher interest rates. Her November 13 remarks separate two potential influences on Bitcoin: relief from disrupted funding and pressure from further monetary tightening.

In the speech, Logan said the Treasury market was functioning very well and presented personal recommendations, rather than announcing an intervention or an adopted Federal Open Market Committee program. She said intervention should be reserved for extreme failures in intermediation; high or rapidly rising yields alone would not justify it.

Her rate outlook points toward further tightening. In November 10 remarks, Logan described current monetary policy as accommodative and called for at least two further quarter-point increases to make it modestly restrictive. She made the pace conditional on developments. The FOMC's October 28 decision had maintained the target range at 3.75% to 4%; her preferred path is distinct from that committee decision.

Her preferred starting point is lending against Treasury securities. The Fed could supply funding at a rate consistent with its monetary-policy target, supporting financial stability while maintaining the interest-rate stance it considers necessary.

Logan also proposed developing central clearing for the Fed's repo lending. Reducing the balance-sheet costs intermediaries incur when passing funding onward could help that money reach the broader market more efficiently during stress.

Purchases would serve a different need. When lending cannot resolve dysfunction, buying securities could free space on intermediaries' balance sheets so they can keep trading. But purchases are harder to separate from monetary policy because they can push down term premiums and stimulate the economy.

Logan suggested holding market-function purchases in a separate account and committing to sell the securities as soon as possible. She argued that purchases expected to unwind quickly should have much less effect on term premiums than holdings kept for years. That would limit the unwanted stimulus, rather than guarantee its elimination.

That aggregate finding is not a forecast of Bitcoin's response to Logan's proposals.
